No. Your internal network COULD be 192.168.x.x, or 172.x.x.x, or 10.x.x.x. It's just that most devices default to 192.168.1.x. These are non-[publicly]routable IP addresses. If packets hit the gateway addressed for one of these rangers, the gateway/firewall/router will drop them, if they're not part of a connected local subnet. And, as others have pointed out, 127.0.0.1 is just the loopback address of the interface. It does nothing but talk to itself. It's not a usable

Ah...not always. Sometimes. 192.168.x.y, 10.x.y.z,172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 and 169.254.0.0 to 169.254.255.255 (since July 2001) are IP addresses that are reserved for private use. They generally cannot be routed over the public network (internet). Your router that connects you to the internet will perform a function called network address translation and map your private address on the inside of your network to the public address assigned to the outside of your router/firewall. I have seen cable networks that use the 10.x.y.z address to assign to end users equipment so they're doing the translation up stream from the end user.
